title: How tooth decay forms and how fluoride helps

sources.title: Oral health (fact sheet)
sources.note: WHO 出版品只取事實、不改寫

sources.publisher: National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIH)
sources.title: The Tooth Decay Process: How to Reverse It and Avoid a Cavity

facts.text: Oral diseases affect an estimated 3.7 billion people around the world.
According to the Global Burden of Disease 2021 study cited by WHO, untreated tooth decay in permanent teeth is the most common health condition in the world.
Dental plaque is a sticky film without color that is full of bacteria and sits on the teeth.
Bacteria in the mouth use the sugars and starches in food and drinks to make acids.
These acids attack enamel, the hard outer surface of a tooth, by taking minerals out of it.
Saliva contains minerals such as calcium and phosphate that help enamel repair itself.
Throughout the day, teeth keep losing minerals and getting them back.
When acid keeps attacking, the repeated loss of minerals can show up as a white spot, an early sign of decay.
Decay at the white-spot stage can still be stopped or reversed, because saliva and fluoride can put minerals back.
If the decay goes on, so much enamel is lost that a cavity forms; a cavity is permanent damage that a dentist treats with a filling.
Eating or drinking sugary or starchy things often gives the acids more chances to attack the teeth.
Fluoride, which comes from toothpaste, tap water with fluoride added, and other sources, helps enamel repair itself and makes it better at resisting acid.
Fluoride also lowers the ability of bacteria to make acid.
WHO says getting enough fluoride is essential for preventing tooth decay and recommends brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.
WHO advises a diet low in free sugars; free sugars include sugars added to food and drinks as well as the sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juices.
High sugar intake, too little fluoride and not removing plaque by brushing can lead to tooth decay, pain, tooth loss and infection.
